lines.text: "The Lord is my portion"; that means, I confess my faith
in the Lord, in my God. He is my portion, which is to say:
if I am confronted by the choice and we are all confronted
by this choice) —here reigns God in all His inscrutability and
terror, God in the majesty of His sovereign will, with His
inexorable command, and irrevocable decrees—there,
the sway of the world with all that it can give, the possibilities
which entice my desire and set a goal to my strivings; if I am
confronted by this choice, then "the Lord is my portion"
it is the Lord whom I choose. I choose the Lord although
then I am building only upon faith and hope and have
nothing visible and tangible in my hands; although then
I can foresee and calculate nothing, and, humanly speaking,
stand wrapped in complete darkness; although then, with all
my plans and activities, I must ever make the reservation:
"As God shall guide, so will I walk,
Resigning all self-will."
The leading image in this poem was furnished by an ancient
narrative concerning Moses. It was not granted to Moses to
see God face to face; as the glory of God passed by, he was
permitted to see only God's back:
"As God shall guide, so will I walk,
Though hard and thorny be the way:
No man shall see His face and live—
Our sunset is His dawn of day."
Luther says in his commentary on the Letter to the Romans:
"It is always the case that we understand our own work
before it is accomplished; God's work, however, we only
understand after it has been accomplished" (II, 205, 5ff.).
"For it is necessarily so, that God's work is concealed, and is
not understood when it comes to pass. It is always hidden
under a form which is the opposite of our human conception"
(11, 204, IIfl.). "What is our good, is concealed from us and
in fact so deeply concealed that it is disguised under its
opposite. Thus our life is hidden under the form of death;
